task_5_extended_text.title: Filming on the Edge: Elena Vance
task_5_extended_text.instruction: Read the article about wildlife documentary filmmaker Elena Vance, and answer questions 13–17.
task_5_extended_text.passage:
Wildlife filmmaker Elena Vance has spent twenty years capturing endangered fauna in the world's most inaccessible habitats. Raised in rural Scotland by naturalist parents, Elena developed an early reverence for the natural world. "My peers spent their teenage years glued to television screens," Elena recalls, "whereas I was tracking badger setts across frostbitten moorlands with my father's 35mm camera." After graduating with a zoology degree, she resisted the temptation of secure laboratory research, opting instead for freelance camerawork.

Her breakthrough arrived in 2012 while filming snow leopards in the high Pamir Mountains. Temperatures routinely plunged below minus thirty degrees Celsius, and weeks passed without a solitary sighting. "In wildlife cinematography, sheer technical brilliance counts for very little if you lack psychological endurance," Elena explains. "The camera operator who packs up after five shivering hours is the one who misses the two-second hunt that defines the entire series." Her perseverance was rewarded when she filmed an unprecedented sequence of a female leopard guiding two cubs across a glacial ridge.

Despite international acclaim, Elena remains critical of certain contemporary industry trends. In particular, she voices reservations about the growing reliance on computer-generated imagery (CGI) and digital sound enhancement in nature documentaries. "When producers artificially manipulate bird calls or amplify footsteps to heighten theatrical tension, they inadvertently sever the audience's genuine bond with reality," she asserts. "Spectators start expecting wildlife to behave like Hollywood actors, which breeds impatience toward authentic conservation efforts."

Today, Elena devotes substantial time to mentoring young filmmakers from biodiversity-rich developing nations. Through her mobile academy, she provides camera gear and storytelling workshops to aspiring directors across East Africa and Southeast Asia. "Indigenous observers possess intuitive ecological knowledge accumulated over generations," Elena concludes. "True conservation storytelling cannot simply be parachuted in by foreign production crews; it must be cultivated from within the communities who coexist with these ecosystems daily."

task_5_extended_text.title: The Granite Solitude of Dartmoor
task_5_extended_text.instruction: Read the memoir and answer questions 13–17.
task_5_extended_text.passage:
For centuries, the desolate granite uplands of Dartmoor in southwest England have cast a somber spell over poets and wanderers. Clothed in purple heather, treacherous peat bogs, and eerie stone monuments dating back to the Bronze Age, this landscape resists human domestication. Last November, seeking respite from the frictionless routine of urban consulting, I packed a canvas rucksack and set out on a four-day solo trek across the north moor without GPS assistance, relying strictly on an Ordnance Survey contour map and an antique brass compass.

By mid-afternoon on my second day, an impenetrable blanket of Atlantic sea-fog rolled silently across the tors. Within minutes, visible landmarks vanished. In such disorienting isolation, every sensory stimulus contracts to the immediate radius of your boots: the squelch of saturated moss beneath wet leather, the sharp whistling of cold gale-force winds through granite crevices, and the brooding silence of the hills. You are no longer a detached observer consuming scenery, but a humble organism navigating raw geological antiquity.

Navigating Dartmoor's infamous mire beds demands rigorous vigilance. What appears to be an inviting patch of bright emerald turf is frequently a deceitful "quaking bog"—a liquid slurry of subterranean silt and decomposed peat. Learning to read subtle botanical indicators became my lifeline: avoidance of fluorescent mosses, following the sturdy hoof-paths carved by wild semi-feral ponies, and probing suspicious ground with a seasoned hazel walking stick.

As dusk settled on the final evening, I reached the ancient oak woodland of Wistman’s Wood. Here, dwarf pedunculate oaks have grown for millennia, their gnarled, moss-encrusted branches contorted like petrified sea serpents between colossal boulders. Standing amidst this primeval cathedral, I was struck by how contemporary society has banished darkness and silence from daily life. We congratulate ourselves on instantaneous digital connectivity, yet we have severed our ancestral relationship with the unhurried rhythms of the earth. Dartmoor does not flatter human self-importance; it humbles our hurried ambitions and reminds us of the profound restorative dignity found in quiet endurance.

task_5_extended_text.title: Echoes from the Ice Margin
task_5_extended_text.instruction: Read the Arctic field memoir and answer questions 13–17.
task_5_extended_text.passage:
Svalbard in late September is a landscape rendered in charcoal, slate, and bone. As our three-person glaciological survey team pitched our geodesic tent upon the gravelly terminal moraine of the Nordenskiöld Glacier, the temperature was already descending toward minus fifteen. We had journeyed to this remote high-Arctic fjord not to measure surface melting with orbital radars, but to document something far more elusive: the internal acoustic and structural memory of ancient ice.

Most people imagine glaciers as inert, frozen monuments. In reality, an active glacier is an animate, restless organism in perpetual motion. Throughout the polar night, the ice fabric groans under immense tectonic pressures. As we hammered seismic listening stakes into the glacier’s snout, the ground vibrated with concussive snaps and low-frequency resonant thrums. These acoustic pulses represent the release of strain energy accumulated over hundreds of years of compaction. To sit alone in total Arctic stillness and listen to a glacier exhale is an experience of terrifying majesty.

On our fourth morning, a sudden katabatic storm ripped down the valley off the inland ice cap, howling at sixty knots and reducing visibility to arm's length in stinging spindrift. For forty-eight hours, our fragile nylon shelter was our entire universe. Confined to our sleeping bags, cooking over a sputtering kerosene stove, we were forced into a state of acute mental endurance. In such extreme isolation, one's perception of time expands; the frantic urgency that governs contemporary metropolitan life is shown to be a trivial illusion against the monumental timescales of the polar wilderness.

When the storm finally spent itself, we emerged into a world bathed in eerie golden twilight. The newly cleared air revealed fresh calving scarps along the glacier’s marine terminus, towering cliffs of turquoise ice that had sheared off into the fjord during the blizzard. Extracting ice core samples from these exposed strata was like reading an illuminated manuscript of prehistoric atmospheres. As I held a translucent core cylinder toward the low Arctic sun, watching tiny ancient atmospheres effervesce in my palm, I felt an overpowering blend of scientific awe and acute grief for a frozen heritage disappearing before our eyes.

[B] To investigate internal acoustic stresses and structural behaviors within the ice.

task_5_extended_text.title: Algorithmic Translation and Sociolinguistic Nuance
task_5_extended_text.instruction: Read the academic essay on artificial intelligence and sociolinguistics, and answer questions 13–17.
task_5_extended_text.passage:
In recent years, neural machine translation (NMT) architectures have achieved unprecedented fluency in standard written registers. Leveraging transformer-based large language models trained on billions of bilingual sentence pairs, contemporary translation engines navigate syntactic inversions and technical vocabularies with remarkable statistical precision. However, computational sociolinguists caution that this apparent technical triumph masks a profound vulnerability: the inability of algorithmic systems to interpret dialectal variation, localized idioms, and pragmatic implicature.

Language is rarely a neutral vehicle for transmuting propositional logic; rather, it functions as an intricate index of social identity, regional heritage, and class allegiance. When machine translation engines process vernacular dialects—such as African American Vernacular English (AAVE), Scots, or Singlish—they routinely stumble over non-standard grammatical markers. For example, the habitual 'be' in AAVE conveys an aspectual nuance of recurring action that standard English accomplishes through auxiliary adverbials. Algorithms trained almost exclusively on sanitized parliamentary proceedings and corporate press releases frequently mistranslate habitual 'be' as a momentary present state, inadvertently flattening crucial temporal distinctions.

This linguistic blind spot creates what sociolinguists term 'epistemic flattening'. By defaulting to hegemonic national standards whenever ambiguity arises, algorithmic translation platforms subtly discourage linguistic diversity. In global commercial and legal environments where machine translation is deployed as a cost-effective triage tool, communications framed in regional vernaculars risk being flagged as erroneous or unprofessional. Consequently, speakers of marginalized dialects face systematic communicative friction, pressured to abandon their heritage varieties in favor of algorithms-friendly standard dialects.

Professional human translators observe that post-editing machine-generated output for non-standard prose is frequently more labor-intensive than translating from scratch. While statistical engines excel at syntactic parsing, they lack the embodied cultural knowledge required to decipher sarcasm, double entendres, and community-specific honorifics. Until computational models incorporate ethnographic context and sociolinguistic sensitivity, translation must remain fundamentally rooted in human interpretation.

task_5_extended_text.title: Urban Soundscape Ecology & Architectural Psychoacoustics
task_5_extended_text.instruction: Read the architectural analysis on urban sound design, and answer questions 13–17.
task_5_extended_text.passage:
For more than a century, municipal approaches to urban sound have been defined by an obsession with acoustic elimination. Noise abatement ordinances, heavy roadside sound barriers, and triple-glazed windows all operate under a singular premise: that the acoustic signature of the city is an inherent pollutant that must be extinguished. However, a growing cohort of architectural psychoacousticians argues that this decibel-reduction paradigm is fundamentally flawed. Complete silence in dense metropolitan spaces is not only physically unachievable, but psychologically disorienting for human occupants.

Soundscape ecology posits that the quality and composition of sonic stimuli exert far greater influence on human neurophysiology than absolute volume alone. While intermittent, unpredictable mechanical impulses—such as sirens, pneumatic drills, and accelerating exhaust systems—trigger immediate cortisol surges and sympathetic nervous arousal, continuous natural sounds produce the opposite effect. Biophilic acoustic interventions, such as cascade fountains, rustling ornamental grasses, and engineered wind corridors, introduce stochastic 'pink noise' that effectively masks harsh mechanical transients without raising overall sound pressure.

Recent residential trials in Amsterdam and Singapore have substantiated this thesis through biometric monitoring. In experimental housing blocks retrofitted with acoustic soundscape landscaping—including porous basalt facades and acoustic vegetated balconies—residents reported a thirty percent reduction in subjective stress and exhibited significantly lower nighttime heart rate variability spikes. Remarkably, ambient acoustic monitors confirmed that exterior decibel levels remained virtually identical to control blocks; the crucial difference lay in the acoustic spectral texture.

Nevertheless, urban developers routinely resist integrating psychoacoustic landscaping into early project phases. Acoustic engineering is frequently treated as an afterthought, relegated to remedial insulation once structural framing is already locked in. Pioneering practitioners argue that cities must transition from reactionary noise mitigation to proactive acoustic curation, designing public squares and transit plazas where sound is sculpted as intentionally as light and shadow.

task_6_short_article.passage:
Modern domestic environments are increasingly inundated with consumer possessions. While material abundance is widely equated with prosperity, cognitive psychologists have revealed that excessive domestic clutter exerts a measurable toll on emotional well-being. Neuroimaging studies demonstrate that cluttered physical environments overload the visual cortex, severely impeding the brain’s capacity to process information and regulate stress hormones.

Intriguingly, the psychological impact of clutter is markedly asymmetrical across genders and personality types. Individuals who identify strongly with home management report elevated cortisol levels when surrounded by disorganization, perceiving unaddressed items not merely as physical objects, but as a persistent backlog of unfinished duties. Conversely, those who reframe domestic possessions as sources of historical continuity or creative stimuli remain relatively impervious to clutter-induced anxiety.

task_6_short_article.passage: Few cognitive experiences are as sudden and emotionally vivid as the involuntary recollection triggered by an unexpected scent. Termed the "Proustian phenomenon"—after Marcel Proust's celebrated description of a tea-soaked madeleine unleashing childhood memories—this sensory superpower has distinct evolutionary roots. Unlike visual or auditory signals, which pass through the thalamus for cognitive filtering before reaching higher cortical regions, olfactory nerves connect directly to the amygdala and hippocampus, the neurobiological centers governing emotion and associative memory. Because this direct neurological pathway bypasses analytical deliberation, scents evoke memories with unparalleled emotional immediacy and sensory fidelity.

While involuntary isolation can provoke distress, intentional solitude functions as a crucial cognitive crucible for personal growth, self-regulation, and creative breakthrough. Cognitive neuroscientists note that constant social interaction activates the "executive control network." When an individual steps away into quiet seclusion, the brain smoothly transitions to the "default mode network." This neural state facilitates autobiographical memory integration, divergent problem-solving, and existential self-reflection. Far from an empty void, solitude is the mental space where intellectual autonomy takes root.

The transition to decentralized, remote employment has elevated asynchronous communication platforms—such as team messaging applications and collaborative project boards—to organizational staples. Proponents celebrate the freedom from rigid real-time meetings, arguing that asynchronous workflows empower personnel to operate during their individual peak cognitive hours. However, occupational psychologists have identified an insidious counter-phenomenon: the chronic fragmentation of attention.

When team members receive an unpredictable trickle of notifications throughout the working day, the brain remains in a perpetual state of hyper-vigilance. Rather than entering periods of sustained, uninterrupted deep work, knowledge workers switch cognitive tasks an average of once every four minutes. This rapid alternation depletes executive functioning, elevating perceived exhaustion even when objective workload volumes remain moderate. Workplace researchers recommend that enterprises establish clear 'notification-free batching windows' to restore mental stamina.

task_6_short_article.passage:
Deep-sea hydrothermal vents, spewing mineral-laden fluids at temperatures exceeding 350 degrees Celsius under hydrostatic pressures of several hundred atmospheres, were long assumed to be sterile oceanic wastelands. In reality, these abyssal fissures host flourishing ecosystems driven by chemosynthetic extremophiles. Microorganisms known as hyperthermophiles not only survive in these hostile environments, but thrive by utilizing specialized enzymes termed 'extremozymes' whose rigid protein architectures resist thermal denaturation.

Biotechnologists and industrial biochemists are intensely interested in these molecular structures. Standard commercial enzymes utilized in pharmaceutical synthesis, textile bleaching, and biofuel production rapidly degrade when exposed to elevated temperatures or corrosive acidities, necessitating costly cooling systems and chemical stabilizers. Extremozymes derived from vent bacteria operate with peak catalytic efficiency precisely under these punishing conditions, offering a sustainable, energy-efficient path toward green industrial manufacturing.

In the pitch-black waters of the deep ocean, sunlight disappears entirely beyond two hundred meters. Bioluminescence—the biochemical production of light by living organisms—is not a rare curiosity, but the dominant mode of communication in the pelagic realm. (20) [ _________ ].

The chemical reaction powering this illumination typically involves two components: a light-emitting pigment called luciferin and an enzyme known as luciferase. When catalyzed in the presence of oxygen, this reaction releases almost ninety-eight percent of its energy as visible cold light, generating virtually no wasted heat. (21) [ _________ ]. In the open ocean, blue-green wavelengths travel farthest through seawater, which explains why the overwhelming majority of marine light displays conform to this color spectrum.

Marine creatures deploy bioluminescence for a wide spectrum of survival strategies. Many predatory anglerfish dangle glowing fleshy lures directly above their needle-sharp jaws to entice unsuspecting prey. (22) [ _________ ]. By emitting faint light from their bellies that precisely matches the intensity and wavelength of downwelling sunlight, midwater squid render their silhouettes invisible to predators lurking beneath them.

Other species utilize sudden, blinding flashes as an emergency defensive smokescreen. Deep-sea comb jellies and brittle stars discharge clouds of glowing mucus to disorient attackers while they make their escape. (23) [ _________ ]. This alarm summons even larger apex predators to attack the initial assailant, effectively saving the glowing prey in the chaos.

Today, biomedical researchers are adapting these natural light-generating systems for human healthcare. By inserting jellyfish bioluminescent genes into human cancer cells, oncologists can track tumor growth and evaluate drug effectiveness in real time under specialized microscopes. (24) [ _________ ]. What began as an evolutionary adaptation in deep-sea obscurity has transformed into an indispensable beacon illuminating modern medicine.

Medieval illuminated manuscripts represent some of humanity's most visually stunning and fragile cultural artifacts. Crafted from animal vellum and decorated with ground mineral pigments and gold leaf, these books have survived for centuries in monastic vaults. (20) [ _________ ]. As conservation science matures, specialists are turning to non-destructive chemical analysis to decelerate this deterioration.

One of the primary agents of destruction is iron gall ink, which served as the standard writing medium across Europe from the Middle Ages through the nineteenth century. Created by combining iron sulfate with oak gall extracts, the ink produces a rich, durable dark line. (21) [ _________ ]. To combat this corrosive pathway, conservators previously bathed entire folios in chemical neutralizing washes. (22) [ _________ ]. Early aqueous immersions frequently caused organic binder adhesives to dissolve, leading to catastrophic flaking of delicate illuminated gilding.

Modern preservation protocols therefore avoid invasive chemical baths whenever possible. Instead, technicians deploy non-invasive portable X-ray fluorescence (XRF) spectroscopy to map elemental distributions across the ink without physical contact. (23) [ _________ ]. Armed with this quantitative diagnostic map, conservators can pinpoint precisely which areas require micro-targeted antioxidant consolidation.

Environmental climate control remains the final, and most critical, line of defense. By maintaining storage vaults at a strict forty-five percent relative humidity and fifteen degrees Celsius, institutions prevent both vellum cockling and fungal germination. (24) [ _________ ]. Through this convergence of chemistry and microclimate management, these ancient voices will endure for future generations.

task_8_gapped_paragraphs.title: The Architecture of Silence
task_8_gapped_paragraphs.instruction: Read the text about acoustic ecology. Choose the correct paragraph from A–F for each gap (25–29).
task_8_gapped_paragraphs.passage:
We inhabit an increasingly deafening civilization. From the perpetual hum of highway traffic to the relentless background churn of ventilation units, anthropogenic noise has permeated virtually every terrestrial ecosystem. While industrial noise was historically treated as an inevitable byproduct of economic progress, acoustic ecologists now recognize chronic sonic saturation as an insidious pollutant that fragments natural habitats and compromises human health.

(25) [ _________ ]

Field studies in national parks have documented this acoustic displacement in striking detail. In coniferous forests bordered by highways, songbirds are forced to alter their singing frequencies or elevate their vocal volume—a phenomenon known as the Lombard effect—merely to communicate territorial boundaries and attract mates. For species unable to shift their acoustic pitch, the consequences are dire: breeding success plummets, and entire populations abandon otherwise pristine nesting grounds.

(26) [ _________ ]

In urban centers, the human consequences of this acoustic assault are equally profound. Epidemiological research links long-term exposure to urban noise with sleep disturbance, impaired cognitive development in children, and heightened risks of cardiovascular disease. The human auditory system never sleeps; even during unconsciousness, the brain processes ambient decibels, interpreting sudden spikes as evolutionary alarm signals that trigger elevated heart rates and stress hormone release.

(27) [ _________ ]

Rather than viewing soundproofing solely as an engineering chore of building thicker walls, visionary planners are embracing "positive soundscape design." This methodology involves strategically integrating natural acoustic elements into civic architecture. Flowing water in civic plazas, gravel walkways, and rustling native foliage do not eliminate decibels, but mask harsh mechanical frequencies with restorative auditory cues.

(28) [ _________ ]

Furthermore, international legal frameworks are beginning to reflect this acoustic consciousness. Several European municipalities have established designated "Quiet Areas" where motor vehicle access is curtailed, and commercial developments must undergo rigorous acoustic impact audits before receiving construction permits.

(29) [ _________ ]

Preserving the integrity of natural soundscapes is not a sentimental indulgence; it is a fundamental pillar of ecological stewardship and human dignity in an overstimulated century.

task_8_gapped_paragraphs.title: The Philosophical Evolution of Cartography
task_8_gapped_paragraphs.instruction: Read the essay on cartography and epistemology. Choose the correct paragraph from A–F to fit each gap (25–29). There is one extra paragraph.
task_8_gapped_paragraphs.passage:
Maps are commonly regarded as objective, scientific mirrors of physical geography. When modern travellers glance at smartphone navigation screens, they operate under the intuitive assumption that satellite coordinates and digital cartography present an unmediated depiction of terrain. Yet historians of science have long demonstrated that cartography is never a purely passive reflection of reality; it is an active act of visual rhetoric and political assertion.

[ Paragraph Gap 25 ]

During the European Renaissance, maritime expansion demanded a transition from theological symbolism to functional navigational geometry. Navigators setting sail into open ocean could no longer rely on aesthetic coastline sketches. This operational necessity culminated in the landmark 1569 world map by Gerardus Mercator, which resolved a vexing mathematical challenge: how to project the surface of a spherical planet onto a flat sheet of parchment while preserving constant compass bearings as straight lines.

[ Paragraph Gap 26 ]

However, this mathematical convenience came with an enormous optical distortion that profoundly shaped geopolitics for centuries. Because the Mercator projection inflates landmasses progressively as they approach the poles, equatorial continents appear drastically diminished. Greenland appears equivalent in size to Africa, despite the African continent being fourteen times larger. For generations of schoolchildren and colonial administrators, this visual distortion reinforced Eurocentric imperial ideologies by exaggerating the territorial prominence of northern imperial powers.

[ Paragraph Gap 27 ]

This critique gained significant traction in the 1970s with the publication of the Peters projection, which prioritized proportional land area over navigational angles. While cartographers debated its aesthetic inelegance, the controversy successfully exposed mapmaking as an epistemological battleground. Maps were finally recognized by the general public not as immutable facts, but as selective arguments designed to serve specific societal priorities.

[ Paragraph Gap 28 ]

Digital geospatial algorithms now curate what information is rendered visible or omitted based on corporate profitability. A search query for an urban district highlights sponsored retail establishments and highway arteries, while obscuring historical landmarks, informal settlements, and low-income residential tracts. The digital map presents a seamless, authoritative veneer, yet it subtly conditions users to perceive urban space through a commercial lens.

[ Paragraph Gap 29 ]

Ultimately, cartography must be understood as an exercise in ethical discernment. To read a map critically is to interrogate what has been centered, what has been pushed to the periphery, and whose interests are legitimized by its boundaries.

task_8_gapped_paragraphs.title: Deep-Time Stratigraphy and the Anthropocene
task_8_gapped_paragraphs.instruction: Read the geological critique on deep time and Earth history. Choose the correct paragraph from A–F to fit each gap (25–29). There is one extra paragraph.
task_8_gapped_paragraphs.passage:
Geological time scales operate on an unimaginably vast horizon compared to human historical chronicles. The rock strata beneath our feet record four and a half billion years of volcanic cataclysms, continental collisions, and evolutionary transformations. Stratigraphers divide this unfathomable expanse into standardized units—eons, eras, periods, and epochs—demarcated by physical shifts in rock composition and fossilized bio-markers.

[ Paragraph Gap 25 ]

Traditionally, establishing a new geological epoch requires locating a Global Boundary Stratotype Section and Point (GSSP), informally known as a 'golden spike'. This physical rock outcrop must exhibit an unambiguous, globally synchronous geochemical or paleontological signal that can be recognized in sediment cores across continents for millions of years into deep time.

[ Paragraph Gap 26 ]

Yet in 2000, Nobel laureate Paul Crutzen proposed an unprecedented departure from standard stratigraphic conventions. He argued that human industrial activity has permanently altered the Earth's biogeochemical cycles to such an extent that the current Holocene epoch has come to an end, succeeded by a new epoch: the Anthropocene.

[ Paragraph Gap 27 ]

Advocates of formalizing the Anthropocene pointed to distinct mid-twentieth-century geochemical markers associated with the 'Great Acceleration'. Chief among these was radioactive fallout from atmospheric thermonuclear detonations in the early 1950s, which deposited synthetic plutonium isotopes globally in ocean sediments, glacial ice, and lakebeds.

[ Paragraph Gap 28 ]

However, the International Commission on Stratigraphy recently voted against officially adding the Anthropocene to the standard geological time scale. Stratigraphic traditionalists argued that human impact is an ongoing, non-synchronous diachronic process spanning millennia of deforestation and agriculture, rather than a single neat boundary stratum.

[ Paragraph Gap 29 ]

Whether classified as a formal geological epoch or an ongoing environmental crisis, the concept of the Anthropocene has fundamentally reshaped human self-understanding. It reminds civilization that human actions are no longer merely cultural, but are now operating as a planetary geologic force.

[C] This proposal sparked fierce contention within the scientific community, pitting conservative field stratigraphers against Earth systems scientists seeking to sound the alarm on global climatic disruption.
[D] Commercial mining conglomerates have heavily lobbied environmental ministries to halt the designated protection of pristine mineral reserves.

task_9_multiple_matching.passage:
[A] Nadia Rossi — Autonomous Light Rail Designer
"The future of mass transit lies in autonomous, on-demand light rail vehicles running on dedicated, grade-separated tracks. Unlike conventional subways that require billions in subterranean tunneling, modular elevated light rail can be rapidly erected over existing highway medians. By coordinating train frequency dynamically through predictive artificial intelligence, we eliminate timetable delays and slash energy waste during off-peak hours."
[B] Marcus Chen — Active Pedestrianization Strategist
"Technological fixes like autonomous cars or futuristic pods miss the core urban reality: geometry. Cities simply lack the physical ground space to accommodate personal vehicles, regardless of their propulsion source. The only scalable, health-affirming solution is aggressive street reallocation: stripping away multi-lane thoroughfares in favor of wide pedestrian promenades and physically protected cycle lanes. When walking and cycling become the safest, fastest travel modes, vehicular congestion vanishes naturally."
[C] Dr. Soren Lindqvist — Dynamic Congestion Pricing Econometrician
"Civic planners frequently ignore economic incentives. As long as urban road space is treated as a free public commons, motorists will inevitably overconsume it until gridlock ensues. Installing dynamic electronic toll gantries that adjust road usage charges in real time based on instantaneous traffic density immediately rationalizes demand. Revenues generated from peak congestion pricing can then be ring-fenced to subsidize regional bus transit for low-income commuters."
[D] Elena Rostova — Intermodal Suburban Hub Architect
"Metropolitan planners obsess over downtown city centers while ignoring suburban transit deserts where seventy percent of commuters actually reside. Our priority must be constructing intermodal park-and-ride interchanges at peripheral ring-road junctions. These hubs combine high-speed suburban express buses, electric vehicle charging depots, and micro-mobility rentals under one roof, providing a seamless bridge between sprawling residential neighborhoods and the urban core."

task_6_monologue_gaps.title: Coral Reef Restoration
task_6_monologue_gaps.instruction: Write NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS for each gap.

questions.stem: 15. Before launching the project, the research team searched for coral colonies with natural _______________________________.
questions.trap: Audio: 'resilient coral colonies that possessed natural thermal tolerance'.

questions.stem: 16. The cutting technique known as micro-fragmentation triggered the corals' _______________________________, accelerating growth rates.
questions.trap: Audio: 'stimulated an innate healing mechanism that accelerated their growth rate'.

questions.stem: 17. Mature fragments were secured onto the ocean floor using a non-toxic _______________________________.
questions.trap: Audio: 'affixed to degraded reef substrates using a non-toxic marine adhesive'.

questions.stem: 18. To control smothering algae, researchers introduced native _______________________________ to act as natural grazers.
questions.trap: Audio: 'we introduced native herbivorous sea urchins, which acted as natural cleaners'.

questions.stem: 19. Dr. Hughes emphasizes that the project's ultimate metric of long-term success is _______________________________ rather than acreage.
questions.trap: Audio: 'true benchmark of our success won't merely be total reef acreage, but genetic diversity'.

task_6_monologue_gaps.title: The Kronan-Nord Baltic Shipwreck
task_6_monologue_gaps.instruction: Write NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS for each gap.

questions.stem: 15. Ship timbers survived intact due to low water salinity and completely _______________________________, preventing shipworm.
questions.trap: Low salinity and complete anoxic sediments prevent shipworm.

questions.stem: 16. Fragile items in the captain's quarters were cleared using an innovative dredge operated by _______________________________.
questions.trap: Specialized gentle water-dredge operated via controlled hydrostatic suction.

questions.stem: 17. Chemical analysis revealed the pitch was infused with pine resin and _______________________________.
questions.trap: Resinous pitch infused with pine resin and juniper oils.

questions.stem: 18. Recovered waterlogged oak timbers were stabilized by immersion in an aqueous bath of _______________________________.
questions.trap: Aqueous bath of polyethylene glycol synthetic wax displaces trapped water.

questions.stem: 19. The wreck provides rare material proof of undocumented _______________________________ between Scandinavia and the Levant.
questions.trap: Material evidence of undocumented maritime trade networks between Scandinavia and Levant.

task_6_monologue_gaps.title: Temperate Celtic Rainforests
task_6_monologue_gaps.instruction: Write NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS for each gap.

questions.stem: 15. Temperate rainforests depend on hyper-humid conditions fostered by the _______________________________.
questions.trap: Hyper-humid microclimates shaped by the Gulf Stream.

questions.stem: 16. Epiphytic lichens are vulnerable because they absorb nutrients straight from _______________________________.
questions.trap: Lack roots and absorb nutrients straight from atmospheric moisture.

questions.stem: 17. Ancient woodland lichens like Sticta are decimated by _______________________________ from traffic and agriculture.
questions.trap: Chronic nitrogen pollution from agricultural runoff and vehicular exhaust.

questions.stem: 18. Natural recolonization across fragmented forests is impeded because many lichens have very _______________________________.
questions.trap: Heavy spores with very limited dispersal radii travelling under 100 meters.

questions.stem: 19. Researchers are trialling _______________________________ to attach small lichen thalli to trees in regenerating corridors.
questions.trap: Trialling micro-translocation strategies: affixing minute lichen thalli to trees.

task_6_monologue_gaps.title: Municipal Wastewater Recycling Infrastructure
task_6_monologue_gaps.instruction: Listen to the presentation on municipal wastewater recycling systems. Complete each sentence with a word or short phrase from the recording. (2 plays maximum)

questions.stem: 15. Incoming wastewater first flows across rotary [          ] screens to extract coarse debris and plastics.

task_1_narrative.title: Task 1: Formal Workplace Mediation
task_1_narrative.prompt: You are a team leader in a publishing house. Two senior editors on your team have had a significant professional disagreement regarding the editorial direction of a flagship literary journal, causing delays in publication. Write an email to your department head explaining the root cause of the friction, summarizing the mediation steps you have undertaken, and proposing a compromise schedule to ensure the journal meets its deadline.

task_1_narrative.title: Task 1: Academic Conference Grant Report
task_1_narrative.prompt: You recently received a travel grant from your university's academic research board to present a paper at an international linguistics symposium. Write a formal report to the grant committee summarizing your paper's reception, detailing two significant methodological insights gained from peer discussions, and outlining how this experience will enrich your department's upcoming seminar series.

task_1_narrative.title: Task 1: Facilities Disruption Compensation
task_1_narrative.prompt: You are the manager of an independent co-working space. Unexpected plumbing and electrical renovations forced the temporary closure of the primary meeting suites for four days, disrupting several client presentations. Write a professional letter to all registered members explaining the structural emergency, offering appropriate commercial compensation, and detailing preventative maintenance upgrades underway.

task_1_narrative.title: Task 1: Heritage Site Advisory Proposal
task_1_narrative.prompt: You are an assistant conservation officer at a regional archaeological site. Recent surges in tourist foot traffic have caused noticeable erosion to ancient sandstone staircases and masonry. Write a formal proposal to the regional heritage director recommending two visitor-flow management solutions and outlining a community volunteer monitoring program.

task_1_narrative.title: Task 1: Clinical Trial Participant Recalibration
task_1_narrative.prompt: You are the head coordinator for a clinical trial investigating a new nutritional supplement. Due to updated ethical guidelines from the institutional review board, participant monitoring protocols must be modified. Write a clear, reassuring letter to study participants explaining the updated appointment frequency and addressing potential privacy concerns.

task_1_narrative.title: Task 1: University Exchange Program Evaluation
task_1_narrative.prompt: You have recently completed a semester abroad at a partner university under an academic exchange scholarship. Write a formal evaluation letter to the international relations office outlining the academic benefits, identifying logistical challenges encountered with housing, and suggesting improvements for incoming cohorts.

task_1_narrative.title: Task 1: Municipal Eco-Audit Recommendation
task_1_narrative.prompt: You are an environmental consultant hired by a district council to audit commercial energy waste in civic administrative complexes. Write an executive summary memorandum to the council president highlighting two major sources of thermal inefficiency and proposing a phased retrofitting strategy.

task_1_narrative.title: Task 1: Museum Exhibition Loan Negotiation
task_1_narrative.prompt: You are a curator at a regional historical museum planning a centenary exhibition on industrial maritime history. Write a formal loan request letter to the keeper of collections at a national maritime museum requesting the display loan of three original shipwright blueprints, explaining security measures and climate controls in place.

task_2_discursive.title: Task 2: Algorithmic Authorship & Academic Integrity
task_2_discursive.prompt: With the rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence in academic and literary writing, educational institutions are divided on policy. Some educators advocate for total prohibition to safeguard original critical thinking, while others argue that AI literacy and critical prompt engineering should become foundational curricular requirements. Write an essay evaluating both perspectives and present your reasoned stance on how educational bodies should respond.

task_2_discursive.title: Task 2: Urban Density vs. Suburban Expansion
task_2_discursive.prompt: Faced with severe housing shortages, municipal authorities must choose between constructing high-density vertical apartment towers within established city limits or approving low-density suburban developments on agricultural greenbelts. Write an analytical essay discussing the environmental, economic, and social consequences of both approaches, and argue which strategy provides a more sustainable future.

task_2_discursive.title: Task 2: Mandatory Civic Service for School Leavers
task_2_discursive.prompt: Several nations are actively considering legislation requiring all secondary school graduates to complete one year of mandatory civic service—such as ecological conservation, elderly social care, or disaster relief infrastructure. Proponents assert this fosters social cohesion, while critics view it as an infringement on personal liberty and career progression. Write an essay exploring both sides and state your own view.

task_2_discursive.title: Task 2: Corporate Sponsorship of Scientific Research
task_2_discursive.prompt: As state funding for university scientific research declines, corporate entities are increasingly financing high-stakes biomedical and technological inquiries. Some argue this drives vital rapid innovation, while others contend it inevitably introduces commercial bias and compromises research integrity. Write an essay analyzing both perspectives and provide your own reasoned conclusion.

task_2_discursive.title: Task 2: Cultural Preservation vs. Global Modernity
task_2_discursive.prompt: Globalization and rapid digital connectivity are accelerating the homogenization of indigenous dialects, traditional rituals, and regional customs. Some cultural theorists argue that preserving endangered languages and customs through state subsidies is essential, while others maintain that cultural evolution and integration are natural and beneficial. Write an essay evaluating both perspectives.

task_2_discursive.title: Task 2: Remote Work and Civic Disengagement
task_2_discursive.prompt: The normalization of remote and home-based employment has drastically reduced commuting times and allowed greater personal flexibility. However, sociologists warn that eliminating physical workplace communities weakens broader civic participation, public transit viability, and downtown commerce. Write an essay discussing the broader societal trade-offs of the remote work revolution.

task_2_discursive.title: Task 2: The Monetization of Digital Privacy
task_2_discursive.prompt: Tech corporations defend targeted advertising models by noting that personalized advertising allows vital digital services, search engines, and communication tools to remain completely free for consumers. Critics counter that pervasive biometric and behavioral data harvesting poses existential risks to personal autonomy and democratic discourse. Write an essay evaluating both arguments.

task_2_discursive.title: Task 2: Tourism Taxation and Heritage Protection
task_2_discursive.prompt: To combat over-tourism, several historic cities have implemented steep daily entry levies and hotel surcharges on international visitors. Advocates assert this curbs environmental wear and funds conservation, whereas tourism operators argue it penalizes ethical travelers and harms local businesses. Write an essay analyzing both sides and present your recommendation.
